It's unclear what caused the anomaly, which occurred 10 minutes into flight.
United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an anomaly during its launch today (Nov. 15), resulting in the loss of 40 Amazon internet satellites.
The Vulcan Centaur lifted off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station today at 12:40 p.m. ET (1740 GMT), hauling 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation toward low Earth orbit (LEO). But they never got there.
"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in an update on X today , 50 minutes after launch. "Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today."
Today's launch was supposed to be a bounce-back mission for the Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket.
Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and had four total flights under its belt before today. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024 , and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).
In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addressed the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)
ULA worked hard on that front and got Vulcan ready to return to flight, which finally occurred today after nine months..
"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update .
That nozzle work apparently paid off: The SRBs appeared to perform as expected during today's launch. But a different, more serious problem cropped up today, and Vulcan Centaur could not overcome it.
Today's launch was supposed to help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in LEO, which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.
Amazon Leo will consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Before today, about 400 of them had reached space on 15 launches, which were conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6 . Today's launch was the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.
The Amazon Leo launch was part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that featured the first-ever catch of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.
Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 15 with news of liftoff, then again at 1:45 p.m. ET with news of the anomaly and loss of the mission.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition.
Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else.
These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy.
The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem.
Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve.
I spoke to Leo Wang , the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai , this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China.
Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said.
Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap.
“If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.”
When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang said Chinese companies have already been preparing.
“If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he said. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.”

The company’s Siri AI-powered eyewear is set to be announced at WWDC next year.
Apple’s smart glasses are among the worst-kept secrets in the tech world. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the company’s first model, which will lack augmented reality features , will be announced at June’s WWDC next year. They likely won’t ship right away, however, with Gurman saying only that “glasses shipments would begin before the end of the year.”
Key to their success will be the newly revamped Siri AI, which is adding fine-grained control over apps . By adding those features now and letting developers add support on the iPhone first, it’s hoping that its smart glasses will be able to hit the ground running.
The prototypes, dubbed N50, are currently running a pared-down version of visionOS and a new processor based on its older smartwatch chips. They also have a MagSafe-like charger Gurman describes as “flat, rectangular” and “roughly the size of a Tic Tac,” which can be used even while still wearing the glasses.
In addition to Apple putting an emphasis on style , privacy , and audio quality, the company is also hoping that Wi-Fi connectivity will grant them a certain amount of freedom, despite relying on an iPhone to actually execute many tasks:
The glasses have Wi-Fi, allowing certain functions outside of third-party apps to continue working when the iPhone isn’t nearby. Users could theoretically keep listening to audio over Wi-Fi after walking away from their phones, for instance, though the eyewear won’t operate as a fully independent device. Apple is also emphasizing the sound quality, which employees have said is industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music playback and FaceTime audio communication.

Normal Gossip host Rachelle Hampton is obsessed with I Like to Watch and splurges on good butter.
Rachelle Hampton is a writer and co-owner at Defector Media , and the host of Normal Gossip , a podcast of anonymous listener-submitted stories about everyday drama. Whether that’s lies about luxury wool in a literal knitting circle, the impeachment of a hypocritical HOA president, or a COVID outbreak at a destination wedding with an absurd 25 bridesmaids, each story is unique in its absurdity, yet weirdly relatable.
After years as one of the co-hosts of Slate’s In Case You Missed It , a podcast that required her to be chronically online, Hampton is enjoying being a little more unplugged these days. And she has perhaps the most interesting answer we’ve ever received to the question “what’s worth splurging on?”
What is your most indispensable tool (analog or digital, app or hardware)?
I think it has to be the Notes app. My entire life is in there! My relationship to the Notes app definitely changes depending on what’s going on in my life at the time. Sometimes I just use it to make my grocery lists, but there was also a period of time where I used it to house my weekly to-do list, so it was basically the only thing between me and destruction. I’ve started blog drafts in the Notes app, and I’ve used it to write out particularly fraught text messages. There are recipes I’ve developed in there, as well as passwords and also questions for my doctors. The first note in my phone is from 2018, so it also serves as a nearly decade-long journal, though there are definitely notes that I simply can’t decipher, like why do I have a note from July 2020 that just says “4th floor”?
I absolutely hate texting. (I write all day, I don’t want to do it in my free time!!) But as someone who also refuses to delete their texts, I have to acknowledge that my most significant personal archive is probably in my Messages inbox.
What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?
It’s a tie between Spotify and whatever phone game I’m currently addicted to, which for the last two years has been Township . I’ve never played Sims or Animal Crossing , but I’m told that it’s something like that. I just like planting my little crops.
I maintain inbox zero across my entire digital life, so I close all my tabs after I finish a task. Right now I have three tabs that I will close immediately after finishing this questionnaire: the first is the Google Doc I’m typing in, the second is the landing page for this series , and the third is a Google tab where I just searched Animal Crossing to make sure I had the name right.
It’s a tie between Reddit and YouTube. Hosting a twice-weekly podcast about the internet for three years either gave me some sort of PTSD or cured me of my social media addiction, depending on how you want to look at it. I can’t spend more than twenty minutes max on IG or X or Bluesky without feeling claustrophobic. The exception is when I’m sick, and I let my fever brain rot on IG reels. Otherwise, it just feels like too much information from too many different sources. Reddit and YouTube are both places where I feel somewhat in control of what I’m seeing.
I don’t think I’ve ever been as happy online as I was on Tumblr between 2013 and 2016. I’m always subconsciously chasing that high.
My older brother bought me a tabletop Klipsch Bluetooth speaker for Christmas a couple of years ago, and it’s still going strong. The sound quality is incredible, and the design is super sexy, so it doesn’t immediately read as a Bluetooth speaker, which I love. I hope I never have to replace it.
One of the stances I’m proudest of is that I’ve never (intentionally) used ChatGPT or Midjourney or any of the other generative AI tools / large language models. It’s getting harder and harder to avoid now that Gemini is built into Google and its various products. Stop trying to write my emails, Gemini!! I’ve never been swayed away from my belief that every single AI company owes a bankrupting amount of money to the writers and artists whose work their products are built on. Until that debt is paid, there’s nothing appealing to me about talking to a chatbot or creating a shitty poster.
In 2020, when I was a staff writer at Slate , I spent a [redacted amount of time] methodically charting and ranking all 349 times Stephenie Meyer used the word murmur in her iconic Twilight saga. The idea had been germinating somewhere in the recesses of my brain for over a decade, only to be released by the surprise 2020 release of Midnight Sun. Seeing this blog come to life (shout out Slate’s interactive designer Natalie Matthews-Ramo!) felt like a fever dream come true.
I’ve rewatched every episode of Netflix’s I Like to Watch with drag queens Trixie Mattel and Katya an embarrassing amount of times. There are certain episodes, like this one where Trixie and Katya react to Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery , that I can quote front to back.
I wish I could say something chill and zen like take a cold shower or something, but the truth is when I’m writing and feeling stuck, I usually smoke a little weed, preferably a sativa strain. Getting high gets me out of my own way, which is usually the problem when I’m feeling stuck. It particularly helps with scriptwriting for Normal Gossip because the tone is so conversational, so being a little bit high stops me from over-writing.
When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?
My favorite coffee shop is less than 500 ft from my apartment, so I end up there without my phone at least once a week, either on purpose or by accident.
Butter! With the caveat that I live by myself and don’t bake, so butter lasts a while in my household, but good butter can change a whole meal. It makes eating toast feel like a luxury instead of a chore to be completed between meetings because I’ve forgotten to eat lunch. My floor for butter is Kerrygold, but recently I’ve been loving this French brand called Isigny Sainte-Mère.

We’ve been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones , bird feeders , health trackers , slushy machines , AI mattress pads , you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive , but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves.
If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.
We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader.
It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running.
If you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro . It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone.
If I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not.
If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour , which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out!
Hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not?
The Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying!
This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for!
Ah, Ninja, the premiere company in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances.
Sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you.
What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones…
When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro . Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware.
Best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years.
As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, new tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life.
For about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the work day, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The company recently launched its second device, Brick Night, which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect set-up tailored to your needs.
It’s embarrassing how whole-heartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 AM Pilates now. Who am I?
I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone , Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down… no one tell Apple, please!
The Dumb Phone is particularly usable because it’s not intended to be a complete replacement for your smartphone — it’s more like a companion device that you can take out with you when you want to feel more present in the world but still may need to call an Uber home.
Wearable health trackers are pretty common nowadays, but after reviewing several different rings and wristbands , Aisha has named a winner.
There are a lot of ugly health trackers. And then there’s the Oura Ring 5 , the leading smart ring maker’s first product that’s thin enough to wear without loudly broadcasting to the world that you’re monitoring your heart rate. (For what it’s worth, I tried the RingConn 3 — which is about the same size as Oura Ring 5 — but returned it, unsatisfied. Womp womp.) Aisha notes in her review that the newest Oura ring is more durable, has a better battery life, and looks more premium than its predecessors.

Critics say proposed funding changes will give government more control of state media.
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of the Czech capital to protest against proposed changes to the funding of public service media, which critics fear could weaken broadcaster independence.
Many of the protesters assembled in Letna Park in Prague on Sunday afternoon.
Some of the demonstrators wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers in tribute to an animated character who has introduced Czech Television’s nightly children’s bedtime stories for decades.
Local authorities anticipated a large crowd days before the November 17 holiday commemorating the 1989 Velvet Revolution against Communist rule, which propelled dissident playwright Vaclav Havel to power.
Under the proposed changes introduced last month , the government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis wants to replace the current monthly fee of 205 crowns ($9.45), which is charged to each household, with funding from the state budget.
Opponents say the change will stifle media freedom as it will make the outlets more dependent on the state. The government insists the plan will not affect editorial independence or programme content.
The bill has passed a preliminary vote ⁠⁠in parliament and awaits further debate.
Broadcast workers have been striking against the proposal since June and earlier this month public media employees staged a one-day strike, leading to state media boycotts by artists and students.
The Million Moments for Democracy group organised Sunday’s demonstration and said “Babis and his government obviously think they will get away with anything… that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property”.
The group said the protest might be “the largest public gathering in Czech history”, as organisers expect 400,000 to 600,000 demonstrators.
Although trust in the media is low – about 30 percent to 33 percent according to the latest Reuters Institute Digital News Report – public service journalism is among the most trusted news sources in the country, with Czech Television the most-watched broadcaster across several age groups.
The proposed media reform has attracted international attention: the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have all criticised it.

Estimated 350,000 people rally against plan to scrap licence fees and fund broadcasters from state budget
Hundreds of thousands of Czechs have rallied in Prague to protest against a perceived government attempt to stifle media freedom.
The gathering on Sunday to save the mandatory licence fees that fund Czechia’s public broadcasters drew more than 350,000 people, making it one of the biggest in the country’s history, organisers said.
Many people wore triangular paper hats similar to an animated TV character called Večerníček, a children’s bedtime story mascot who has become a symbol of the protest. Others carried banners saying: “We won’t give media away.”
The event was held at the capital’s Letná Plain, the cradle of the 1989 Velvet Revolution which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.
It marked the latest challenge to the prime minister, Andrej Babiš, and his coalition of populist, hard-right nationalist and Eurosceptic parties, and follows weeks of demonstrations in towns and cities and a strike by staff at Czech TV and Czech Radio.
Protesters say the plan to scrap licence fees and fund the broadcasters from the state budget would give ministers more leverage over newsrooms and follows the example of Hungary, Poland, Serbia and Slovakia , where current and previous rightwing populist governments eroded media independence.
A series of protests has been held since late October, when the first reading of the bill to scrap the licence fees was pushed through in the middle of the night.
The Million Moments for Democracy group, which organised the demonstration, said the authorities would now grasp the level of opposition. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organiser. “It’s just a beginning.”
In a statement, the group demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners posed a threat to democracy. “Babiš and his government obviously think they will get away with anything … that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property,” the group said.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” said one protest banner. “Hands off the media,” said another.
Šárka Dumišincová, a singer, said for her the media represented freedom. “The fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today,” she told the Associated Press.
“We need to keep media independent. The government is taking steps to control them, cut their funding and affect what they broadcast,” computer programmer Jan Snasel told AFP at the rally.
The proposed changes, which would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15%, have drawn fire from international media organisations.
The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have also criticised the government’s media plan, likening it to controversial moves by Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico , and Hungary’s former premier Viktor Orbán .
Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said protesters were riling up the public with unfounded claims about threats to media freedom.
Last week, he published an op-ed on what he called the “seven lies” being peddled by the opposition over the licence fees, which together add up to 205 koruna (£7) a month.
“Anyone who talks about ‘nationalisation’ [of public media] is deliberately lying,” he wrote, describing the criticism as “hysterical outbursts”. “Under no circumstances will we interfere in editorial work.”
Babiš heads a coalition that includes his ANO, or YES, movement, the rightwing Motorists for Themselves and the anti-migrant and pro-Russian Freedom and Direct Democracy party. Despite the protests, ANO still enjoys the backing of about 30% in opinion polls.

The role AI played in job losses at Australia’s NAB, Qantas, Canva and Atlassian is far from clear – but it may prove to have more impact on the stock market than the jobs market
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
I n 1987, the Nobel prize winning economist Robert Solow remarked: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” At the time, computers had been around for 40 years. Real productivity gains did emerge in the 1990s after the arrival of the internet, but they were short-lived.
Four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the pattern seems to be much the same: lots of hype and excitement but with very little productivity growth. The main economic impacts, as in the 1990s dotcom era, have been a stock market boom and huge investment in infrastructure (fibre optics then, datacentres today), betting on future demand that has yet to emerge.
Still, the announcement of large-scale job losses at NAB, Qantas, Canva and Atlassian, some of them explicitly blamed on AI, raises the question of whether the job apocalypse is finally here. The evidence suggests otherwise.
NAB has specifically denied that AI played a role in its decision, and there is no reason to disbelieve this. The NAB sackings seem to be business as usual for the bank which, since 2010, has announced a mass sacking in most years, sometimes more than one. Yet its total employment numbers have remained unchanged, even though many employees have quit or retired.
Quite simply, NAB’s business model, like that of other banks and big employers, is to hire employees when it needs them and sack them whenever it is profitable to do so. That’s capitalism after all, but it’s a far cry from the days when big employers like banks gave and expected loyalty in dealing with their workers.
Qantas has invoked AI but only, I would argue, to muddy the waters. The decision to outsource 850 jobs to India is consistent with the airline’s longstanding strategy of doing over Australian workers while claiming preferential treatment due to being a national flag carrier.
The claim by Qantas that the jobs will eventually be replaced by AI complicates reporting of what is in reality a simple case of offshoring, but if anything it weakens the Qantas case. If the jobs are going to be automated anyway, why go to the trouble of sacking existing staff ahead of time and setting up a new operation overseas? Let’s hope that members of the Australian political class give this some thought as they enjoy the hospitality of the Chairman’s Lounge.
Canva looks more vulnerable. The firm operates on a “software as a service” model, charging monthly annual subscriptions for access to easily usable graphics design software. This has been a highly successful model for users who don’t want to struggle with more powerful but complex packages. Now, however, anyone who wants, for example, a poster advertising an event, can do so in seconds, specifying the style, colour scheme and so on. The result may be recognisable as “AI slop” but many people will settle for that.
Atlassian’s business model is also under challenge, but its software offerings will be harder to replicate with the use of AI. Atlassian’s applications focus on project management and organisation-wide data. Piecemeal use of AI by individual workers is unlikely to replace these functions. It’s possible that AI will enable the reverse engineering of software packages, but this remains to be seen.
Finally, it’s worth observing that the AI hyperscalers themselves, firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic, along with Meta (Facebook/Instagram) and Alphabet (Google), aren’t safe. Cheap “open-weight” models such as DeepSeek (China) and Mistral (France) are running only a year or so behind the leaders, while investing a small fraction of the money. It’s entirely possible that LLMs (large language models) will become like email, an essential part of life for many people but not a source of profit. If that’s the case, we are more likely to see an apocalypse in the stock market than in the jobs market.
John Quiggin is a professor at the University of Queensland’s school of economics

Nine people were killed in the shooting at the Greek Orthodox church last month
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.
The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.
Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".
The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.
Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.
CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.
A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.
It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.
Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation.
"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."
The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.
They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them , the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.
King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".
The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.
Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details.
Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance.
Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.

Ronaldinho played the first 45 minutes for Ravenna against Forli
Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their 2-0 win over Forli in an Italian third-tier derby.
The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.
He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.
The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.
He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.
At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.
Ronaldinho was substituted at the break with the score at 1-0.
A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.
The game was streamed in several countries around the world.
Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.
A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.
In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.
He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.
He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.
Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.
"It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia.
And asked if he might play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group, he said: "If the president calls me, I'll be back."
All of Ravenna's players - and not just the starting XI - posed with Ronaldinho in the team photo before kick-off

Iran and the US are vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz
Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.
The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.
Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".
It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.
The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.
Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.
As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.
Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."
In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."
Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.
The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.
Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

Ronaldinho played 45 minutes on his return to professional football in Italy. The 46-year-old Brazil great announced in June that he had signed for the Serie C side Ravenna, 11 years after he appeared to have brought his illustrious career to a close with Fluminense.
Five months later, he was in the starting lineup as Ravenna faced their local rivals Forlì. Ronaldinho, wearing the No 10 shirt, entered the stadium to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Stadio Bruno Benelli adding a temporary 1,800-capacity stand – dubbed “R10” – for the occasion. Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli’s Con Te Partiro blasted out of the stadium’s speakers.
Ronaldinho failed to add to his goal tally upon his return, showing some nice touches and playing a role in helping Giulio Donati score Ravenna’s opening goal, but unable to create a sight of goal for himself.
The 2005 Ballon d’Or winner acknowledged the Ravenna fans at the end of the first half and was replaced by Matteo Maggio when the teams returned after the break.
Ronaldinho, who has also become a shareholder in the club, hinted there could be more appearances to come, telling Sky Italia: “It went by too fast, that has always been football for me. Is this my last one? I don’t know. If the president keeps calling me, I will come back. It is always a pleasure. I told the president, if he needs me, then I will be here.
“It was lovely to be here, playing, having the buildup in the dressing room. Football has always been the most wonderful thing in my life.”
Ravenna, who have not played in Serie B since 2008, are second in their regional group in Serie C and came into the weekend’s fixtures six points behind the leaders, Spezia.
It is Ronaldinho’s second spell in Italy, albeit at a much lower level, after three seasons with Milan from 2008 to 2011, where he won one Serie A title. He also played for Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona in a trophy-laden career that included claiming the World Cup with Brazil in 2002. He scored 94 goals in 207 matches for Barcelona and 33 times in 97 games for Brazil. He has also played for Brazilian sides Grêmio, Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, and for Querétaro in Mexico.

Strikes cast further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington with increasing risk of escalation
Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain , casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.
Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran .
Meanwhile, in Yemen , Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.
The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.
At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.
US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.
Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.
However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.
A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.
In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.
There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.
The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.
Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.
Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.
The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.
“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.
The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.
In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend ⁠Aden on the southern ​coast.
“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of ‌a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.
The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.
A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.

A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.
Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.
A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".
Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.
The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.
Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".
It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."
Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".
Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.
He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.
The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.
Though a ceasefire was reached last October, Israel has continued strikes it says are targeting remaining Hamas militants, which it argues it has the right to do under the terms of the ceasefire agreement.
More than 1,640 people have been killed in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Update November 15: An earlier version of this article referred to Israel carrying out 'occasional' strikes in Gaza following a ceasefire in October 2025. This word has been removed to better reflect the frequency of Israeli strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire.

Authorities say Russian intelligence service ordered attack Estonian PM links to Tallinn’s support for Ukraine
Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.
On Saturday morning, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defence company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. No injuries or damage were reported after the company’s security team responded to the incident.
Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said on Sunday the attack was carried out “with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire”. Authorities have requested a court order for five of those detained to remain in custody, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported.
The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, said the border closure was needed to reduce the risk of further attacks and “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities” were unacceptable.
He linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine . “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine. Estonia’s response is the opposite. We will strengthen our security, work even more closely with businesses and our allies, increase pressure on Russia and continue supporting Ukraine,” Michal said.
The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the warning, saying : “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”
Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. The authorities did not specify how long the closure would be.
It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence company that authorities have attributed to Russia, after an arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August.
In September, Kapo said it was confident that incident was “a deliberate and pre-planned attack carried out on behalf of Russian special services”. The agency also said it fitted a pattern of Russian attacks targeting defence and drone companies, particularly those with links to Ukraine.
At the time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires over the attack, but the Kremlin denied any link to Russia, saying it was a “baseless” and “ill-considered” accusation “with absolutely no relation to reality”.
Several European intelligence services have repeatedly warned of potential attacks against defence companies and growing Russian attempts to recruit citizens in EU and Nato countries on messaging platforms online to carry out acts of sabotage.
Michal noted that the weekend’s arrests came after security agencies told the defence industry of potential risks. “We do not warn about these threats without reason. Preparedness matters, and this time it clearly paid off,” he said.
The Russian foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, told state news agency Tass: “... If ‌these are ‌their real plans, then ‌they fit into yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia”.

New European Union migration and asylum laws have largely failed to stem the flow of migrants to Spain and its territories.
Spain has declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands after the arrival of more than 9,000 people in its Atlantic Ocean territory since the start of November.
Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said it had rescued 1,488 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, also known as pirogues, most of whom arrived on El Hierro in the Canary Islands from West Africa on Saturday.
That’s broken the record of 1,461 people rescued six years earlier in November 2020.
Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres is visiting ⁠El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the surge in migrant arrivals.
Al Jazeera’s Bernard Smith, reporting from El Hierro, said the arrival this year has set a record in the 32 years since statistics have been collected.
“There’s been even more arrivals by Sunday afternoon”, Smith said, adding that the new arrivals are processed at the port in El Hierro and taken to a reception centre and sent on to other Canary Islands or to the Spanish mainland.
The European Union’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum officially came into force on June 12, 2026, introducing “firm and fair rules” for accepting asylum requests, marking the most sweeping overhaul of EU asylum and border laws in decades.
“EU states are under pressure to do more to control migration from Africa and from outside the European Union,” Smith said, adding that the new rules haven’t stopped the flow of migrants to Spain and its enclaves.
Last month, Spain deported more than a dozen of the 80,000 people who had entered its North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over a 48-hour period in late July.
At least 100 people died during the mass crossing into the autonomous city, which covers just 18.5 square kilometres (7.1sq miles) and has a population of about 80,000.
Most of the migrants arriving in El Hierro depart from West Africa, many leaving from Senegal, with hopes of reaching mainland Europe.
But to get there, they risk their lives in small, often overcrowded boats at sea.
One boat on Saturday was carrying 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children, authorities said.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded at least 450 deaths on the Western African Atlantic route in the first 10 months of 2026.
“It is a treacherous journey,” said Al Jazeera’s Nicolas Haque, reporting from Dakar in Senegal, from where some of the boats depart, adding that favourable weather conditions in the Atlantic Ocean have made departures from the coastlines in Africa much easier in recent years.
“So when the weather conditions allow it, the boats go out there,” he said, noting that migrants use “wooden fishing vessels called pirogues” in which up to 100 people are packed in for “a journey that can last one week”.

90 min Spain have four additional minutes to preserve an unbeaten record stretching back two-and-a-half years.
89 min Lamine crosses … and it’s a goalkick. England bring on Burn for the heroic Ben White, his goal the winner as things stand and his tackle on Lamine to preserve it just as important.
87 min “Even if England somehow scrape through this, the story of the night isn’t how excellent we were for first hour – which we bloody were – but how we managed to stuff/almost stuff it up again,” reckons Christopher Lee.
“Disappointing because this could really have been a turning point for the story of these players and Thomas Tuchel’s England reign. Even if we win from here it’ll still be backs to the wall England scraping through rather than dominate England smash the world champions.”
I respectfully disagree: if england see this out, they’ll have the best of both worlds: a dominant display against the hardest team to do that too, then a backs-to-the-wall rearguard.
86 min This, my mates, has been a proper game of association football. Lamine picks a dink into the box, chested off by Fermin – who, like Pedri, has made a difference – but Porro can only drill wide. If De la Fuente had gone with those three subs from the start, we might’ve seen a different contest.
85 min England are deeper than they’d want to be but Konsa brings them up to the edge then, when Williams skates around the outside, beating Rogers, his cross is nasty … but Porro dives to head wide.
84 min A brilliant pass from Pedri sets Lamine free art inside-left! Is this his moment?! It is not because, out of nowhere, Benjamin White launches into a precision challenge, taking all of the ball and none of the man. That might be the tackle of his life, and could well be crucial.
82 min Spain pass and England drop, but the supine resignation we saw against Argentina isn’t quite there. Changes for England: Spence and Calvert-Lewin for Bellingham and Gordon, which the Madrid man loves just as much as you’d expect.
80 min England are pinned back, too deep – we may have seen this one before. This time, instead of looking to commit a defeder, Lamine waves a low curler from edge, which Trafford dives to fist away – back into play, not around the post. But when the ball comes back, he gets it behind, and the corner comes to nowt.
79 min Spain are getting Lamine on the ball now and he teases Hall, who does really well not to buy what’s being sold, eventually blocking his man off with help from Trafford, and England clear.
78 min There’s such tempo and intensity to this game, and Tuchel acts, taking off Kane and introducing Lewis-Skelly. I can see why he’s done that but, on this occasion, I might’ve kept Kane on as a target man to hold the ball; who is the striker now?
77 min A bit of England possession, Gordon and Bellingham doing well in the inside-left channel, but this time when Bellingham crosses the ball soars behind for a goalkick.
How will England eff it up? Like this. Gordon tarries in possession, Pedri robbing him, then a fantastic first-time pass from Fermin sends Lamine away down the left. His low cross is a delight, Williams arriving on to it without breaking stride, and he swishes a finish in off the near post. It’s a different game now!
73 min Spain win a corner down the right which yields another from the left. This time it goes short and, when the ball is clipped to the far post, Belling ham opts to let it go but Oyarzabal is behind him, and when he forces the cut-back, Fermin shoots … and Trafford parries. Pressure is building…
72 min A further change for Spain , Williams replacing Zubimendi as De la Fuente goes for it.
70 min Spain find Lamine on the right side of the box, but his attempted curler is blocked at source. England have defended superbly so far, the penalty Spain’s first shot on target.
69 min This is a proper test for England; not one Tuchel will have wanted but perhaps one the team needs. If they can make it through this, so wind up dominating Spain with 11, then seeing them away with 10, they’ll end the evening a different side to the one which started it. Lose and – though it’ll hurt – they can blame individual error.
67 min Someone on the England bench is booked, and I wonder if Tuchel contemplates a change. He needs keep an out-ball, but perhaps midfield control means he remove Rogers for, perhaps, Lewis-Skelly.
Oyarzabal ambles up, skips, and when Trafford dives left, he sweeps right. Hold on to your toupees, this is going to be a serious 25 minutes.
64 min That question, eh? How will England eff it up? Like thus: Quansah is mugged by Lamine, the first time England have been so caught, and when Baena sweeps him in, Anderson hauls him back, a rash call, and Spain have a route back into the game!
62 min “Are you Scotland in disguise?” sing the away end, a disbelieving Philip Cornwall back in touch BUT EXCUSE ME WHILE I INTERRUPT MYSELF ONCE MORE!
61 min Gordon, who’s having a fine night, win another corner, and England will fancy another here, but this time Rice’s floaty delivery is easily fielded by Simon.
60 min And what a moment of redemption that is for White. Jeered by his own fans after leaving the World Cp squad in 2022, he’s nicely reintegrated now, and that was the kind of finish you’d expect to see from Pedro Porro. That is some serious praise.
Kane across the face of the box to Bellingham, who caresses in behind for White! He takes a touch, narrowing the angle but forcing the keeper to move then, when Simon spreads himself, he picks a very deliberate finish through the keeper’s legs! This is a hiding!
57 min Spain haven’t lost for 43 games …and BUT EXCUSE ME WHILE I INTERRUPT MYSELF … THEY’RE GOING TO LOSE TONIGHT!
56 min Bellingham, whose good work won the corner from which England scored, wins another ion similar style, this time down the left, as we see footgge of the England goal, Tuchel on the touchline also applying brow to imaginary ball – that’s how much time and space Konsa had. This time, the corner comes to nowt.
54 min Minor Spain protests for a free-kick of some sort, but VAR isn’t interested. Konsa couldn’t have been freer, the question on everybody’s lips a familiar one: how will they eff it up from here?
A Rice outswinger and, in the middle of the box, Konsa has maybe five yards of space all around him to run in and guide home from seven yards. England are all over this!
52 min Zubimendi picks up a poor pass and punches between Anderosn and Rice, finding Lamine … whose trivela cross is straight at Trafford. Then England find Bellingham down the right of the box and he delays well before winning a corner off Pedri, gesticulating to where he thinks the away end is, but isn’t.
51 min Down the right, 30 yards from goal, Rice will swing the free-kick out … and Huijsen heads away well, facing his own goal.
49 min Lamine spreads wide to Cucurella, then Spain work it back to him, Hall delaying before Gordon confiscates possession. Those two have been brilliant so far and, when England counter, Rogers cuts inside Cucurella, who trips him and is booked.
48 min England win it high and win a throw, Tuchel’s alacrity in returning the ball evidencing their intent to speed up the game and impose their will. Spain soon have possession back, but it’s a message not to retreat.
48 min Already, Spain look calmer, Pedri linking play and finding pockets. England will, as Tuchel warned, have to be patient.
47 min “As I’m sure 347 other people are also pointing out,” chortles Bob O’Hara, “Pochettino made a pretty big managerial eff-up this week.”
I fear that lush mane is on borrowed time – on which point is it just me who sees Stan Rizzo from Mad Men?
46 min We go again, those Spain changes reflecting England’s superiority.
A triple Spain change: Huijsen, Pedri and Fermin on; Ruiz, Cubarsi and Merino off.

The pope calls for the preservation of Indigenous traditions in Peru as he wraps a 12-day tour in Latin America.
Pope Leo XIV has criss-crossed Peru on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour, making stops in the Andean highlands and the Peruvian Amazon.
Sunday marked the last full day of his trip, which has seen him visit Uruguay and Argentina already.
The pontiff spent the morning in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire, delivering a speech at the Indigenous fortress of Saqsaywaman.
In his remarks, Leo praised the region’s traditional festivities and processions, which often blend Indigenous and Catholic spirituality.
“The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way,” he said.
Huge crowds also packed Cusco’s central Plaza de Armas to greet Leo. Though born in the United States, Leo acquired Peruvian citizenship in 2015, after living in the country for years and later becoming the bishop of Chiclayo , a major city in the north.
The visit to Cusco, a high-altitude city some 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested the 71-year-old pope’s stamina as he continues to recover from lung cancer surgery.
Leo, however, has shown no sign of fatigue since his 12-day, three-nation South American trip began on November 6.
In the afternoon, Leo flew to Pucallpa, a city near Peru’s eastern border, on the banks of the Ucayali River.
Pucallpa is considered a gateway to the Peruvian Amazon, and during his stay, Leo reinforced his late predecessor Pope Francis’s teachings on protecting the environment.
He also denounced the violence faced by Indigenous land defenders, who use their advocacy to confront deforestation, pollution and the threat of Indigenous expulsion.
“Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said. “The blood of these brothers cries out ⁠to God and demands justice.”
Indigenous communities have long been threatened by illegal mining, deforestation and other forms of exploitation. Mining has also led to a water crisis in Peru, with pollution leading to an increased risk of heavy metal poisoning.

A spokesman for the Southern Armed Forces, a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, said on Sunday that it was redeploying from Dhubab airport and areas around Bab al-Mandeb in southwestern Yemen.
“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats,” the spokesman said.
The announcement raises the prospect of new Houthi advances towards Aden on the southern coast, the base of the internationally recognised government since the Houthis drove leaders from the capital Sanaa more than a decade ago.
Reinforcements would also be sent to try to end the Houthis’ siege of Taiz, where fighting has been raging to the west of the city, the announcement added.
Humanitarian conditions are worsening in Yemen’s third-largest city, with aid supplies blocked from entering and civilians unable to leave.
The city hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen since the 2022 ceasefire collapsed this summer and fighting surged. The Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized large areas of territory along Yemen’s western coast in September.
Sunday’s announcement could signal a setback for the Yemeni government forces’ counteroffensive launched in September to reclaim areas seized by Houthi fighters.
The counteroffensive quickly recaptured key positions around the strait, notably Dhubab, but failed to push the Houthis out of the key city of Mocha and other areas near the coast.
The Houthis responded by intensifying drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, grounding flights and targeting energy facilities.
Earlier on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said it shot down two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh, the Saudi capital. Later, coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said two drones launched over the Mecca region and another over the Medina region. The Houthis denied the allegations they attacked Mecca as “a blatant lie”.
Houthi forces also captured highland areas north of Aden, where the government has been operating since 2015, and say they are preparing to advance on the city itself.
A spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majid Al-Nazili, called on the international community to help return Bab al-Mandeb and Yemen’s west coast to government control, stressing that the strait was of vital importance for freedom of maritime navigation and international trade.
Separately, Yemen’s armed forces said that they had launched 906 strikes against Houthi positions, including 41 air strikes, on Marib, al-Jawf and Taiz.
Also on Sunday, the International Committee of the Red Cross announced that the Houthis, with its support, unilaterally released 600 prisoners “in connection with the armed conflict”.

'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.
"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.
President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.
The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.
On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.
Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.
The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.
He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".
Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.
"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".
"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.
Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

Nearly 2,200 migrants have reached the Canary Islands over the past two days, Spain’s coastguard said Sunday, continuing a recent surge of arrivals from West African countries to the Spanish archipelago, where the authorities declared a migration emergency earlier this week.
Nearly 2,200 migrants have reached Spain’s Canary Islands by boat over the past two days, Spain’s maritime rescue service said on Sunday.
The archipelago off northwest Africa is a major entry point for migrants, mainly from West Africa , attempting the dangerous Atlantic crossing in makeshift boats. More than 13,000 of the just over 28,000 people who arrived in Spain by sea between January and the end of October landed in the Canary Islands, according to the Interior Ministry.
Spain declared a migration emergency on the islands on Tuesday following a rise in arrivals in recent weeks, particularly from sub-Saharan Africa. The country is due to hold an early general election in two weeks.
The rescue service said it had assisted 1,324 people aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom reached El Hierro, an island with a population of 12,000. That figure approached the route’s daily rescue record of 1,461 people, set on November 7, 2020.
Red Cross staff meet migrants at the port, providing dry clothes, food and water and registering their arrival, Dácil León, the organization’s emergency coordinator in Tenerife, told public broadcaster RTVE.
The Atlantic crossing between West Africa and the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. Those journeys can last days or weeks, with most boats departing from Mauritania.
Read more Spain’s Canary Islands overwhelmed by migrant arrivals
In July, tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta in just two days, causing chaos and reigniting debate over immigration in Europe and beyond. More than 140 people died making the journey.
Most of those who crossed left within days, but up to 15,000 remained.

İsa’yı işaretledi. Doğru cevap Hz. Muhammed ’di ve yarışmacı elendi. Sorunun ifadesi ise izleyiciler arasında tartışma yarattı.
Kim Milyoner Olmak İster 'in son bölümünde 1 milyon TL'lik soru ekrana geldi. Yarışmacı Canan Topçu, ilk baraj sorularını zorlanmadan geçti ve 500 bin TL'lik soruyu da doğru yanıtladı. Böylece ATV ekranlarında Cem Öğretir'in sunduğu yarışmada 1 milyon TL'lik soruyu açtırmaya hak kazandı.
Ancak bu aşamada elinde hiç joker kalmamıştı. Ekrana gelen soru ise dini bir bilgiye dayanıyordu: 'Hangi peygambere, Kur'an-ı Kerim'in hiçbir yerinde adıyla hitap edilmemiştir?'
Uzun süre düşünen Topçu, yarışmadan çekilip kazandığı parayla ayrılmak yerine risk almayı seçti. Cevabı B şıkkındaki Hz. İsa oldu.
Doğru cevap ise A şıkkındaki Hz. Muhammed 'di. Yanlış yanıtla birlikte Topçu, 1 milyon TL'lik soruda yarışmaya veda etti ve bu cevap ona büyük bir üzüntü yaşattı. Yarışmanın baraj sistemine göre bu yanlış cevap, kazancın ikinci baraj olan 300 bin TL'ye düşmesi anlamına geliyor; çekilseydi 500 bin TL ile ayrılabilecekti.
Peki doğru cevap neden Hz. Muhammed ? Sorunun kilidi 'adıyla hitap' ifadesindeydi.
Kur'an-ı Kerim'de Hz. Âdem, Hz. Nuh, Hz. İbrahim, Hz. Musa ve Hz. İsa gibi pek çok peygambere doğrudan adıyla seslenilir. 'Ey Musa' ya da 'Ey İsa' gibi hitaplar ayetlerde birçok kez geçer.
Hz. Muhammed'e ise hiçbir ayette 'Ey Muhammed' diye seslenilmez. Ona yönelik hitaplar 'Ey Peygamber' ve 'Ey Resul' gibi sıfatlarla yapılır.
Üstelik ' Muhammed ' adı Kur'an'da tamamen yer almıyor da değil. Âl-i İmrân, Ahzâb, Muhammed ve Fetih surelerinde toplam dört kez geçiyor. Ancak bu ayetlerde ad bir hitap olarak değil, ondan bahsedilirken kullanılıyor.
Yarışmanın ardından soru da en az yanlış cevap kadar konuşuldu. Bazı izleyiciler, 'Muhammed' adı Kur'an'da geçtiği için sorunun hatalı olduğunu öne sürdü.
Öte yandan sorunun 'adı geçmek' değil 'adıyla hitap edilmek' üzerine kurulduğunu hatırlatanlar da oldu. Bu görüşü savunanlara göre ifade doğruydu, ancak yüksek stres altında yanlış anlaşılmaya çok açıktı.

With Christmas approaching, dozens of Father Christmas impersonators swapped their festive grottos for classroom desks in south London on Thursday 12 November , attending a training session designed to make their encounters with children as magical as possible. Dressed in their familiar red suits, the Santas practised saying "Merry Christmas" in sign language, studied the latest toy trends and learned how to respond to unexpected questions from young visitors.
Organised by the Ministry of Fun, Santa School is now in its 28th year , preparing performers for appearances in shopping centres, department stores and festive attractions across the UK and beyond. The lessons also cover more sensitive situations, such as children wishing for separated parents to reunite or sick relatives to recover, where kindness and careful listening matter more than promises.
The training also featured the Ministry of Fun's annual State of Santa report, which offers a glimpse into changing Christmas traditions. According to the organisation's research, bookings for Mrs Claus have risen by 32%, while 60% of children still send physical letters to Father Christmas . Mince pies remain the favourite Christmas Eve offering, appearing on 77% of plates, although kombucha has made its debut on 2% of tables. The report also suggests that a typical visit to Santa lasts just three minutes and 45 seconds , leaving performers little time to create a memorable experience. For veteran Santas, the challenge is not simply knowing the latest toys, but making every child feel heard and preserving the magic of Christmas.
